entry: Thermal electromagnetic radiation emitted by an idealized black body, an object that absorbs all radiation falling on it. A black body's emission is a continuous spectrum that depends only on its temperature, described by [[Planck's law]]. The term *black body* was introduced by [[Gustav Kirchhoff]] in 1860. At room temperature a black body radiates mostly in the [[Infrared|infrared]]; at about 500 °C it begins to glow dull red, and at higher temperatures it emits more orange, yellow, green and blue light. Planets and stars, including the [[Earth]] and [[Sun]], are not perfect black bodies, but black-body radiation is a good first approximation for the energy they emit. In 1900 [[Max Planck]] resolved the ultraviolet catastrophe by proposing that electromagnetic energy is emitted and absorbed in discrete packets, or quanta.

Theoretical stellar remnant, a [[White dwarf|white dwarf]] that has cooled sufficiently to no longer emit significant heat or light. The time required for a white dwarf to reach this state is calculated to far exceed the current age of the [[Universe|universe]] (13.79 billion years), so no black dwarfs are expected to exist at present. A black dwarf would be composed mainly of [[Carbon|carbon]] and [[Oxygen|oxygen]], with trace amounts of neon and magnesium. The term has also been applied to hypothetical cooled [[Brown dwarf|brown dwarfs]].

[[Color|Achromatic color]] resulting from the absence or complete absorption of visible light. Black is often used symbolically to represent darkness, and black and white have long described opposites such as good and evil. Since the [[Middle Ages|Middle Ages]] it has been the symbolic color of solemnity and authority, and judges and magistrates still commonly wear it. Black was one of the first colors used in art, appearing in [[Neolithic|Neolithic]] cave paintings. In the [[Roman Empire|Roman Empire]] it became the color of mourning, and over the centuries it was frequently associated with death, evil and magic. Black is the most common [[Ink|ink]] color for printing books and newspapers because it gives the highest contrast with white paper. As of September 2019, the darkest material is made by MIT engineers from vertically aligned [[Carbon nanotube|carbon nanotubes]].

Fly of the family Simuliidae, sometimes called buffalo gnats or turkey gnats. More than 2,200 species have been formally named, divided into two subfamilies. Adults are usually small, black or gray, with short legs and antennae. They feed mainly on nectar, but the females of most species also feed on the blood of [[Bird|birds]] or [[Mammal|mammals]], including humans, to obtain nutrients for egg production. Their [[Larva|larvae]] live in running water, attached to submerged rocks, and filter-feed on small organic particles, algae and bacteria. Black flies spread several diseases, including river blindness in [[Africa|Africa]] and the Americas, and many U.S. states run programs to suppress their populations.

Highly venomous snake of the family Elapidae, native to [[Sub-Saharan Africa|sub-Saharan Africa]]. First described by Albert Günther in 1864, it is the second-longest venomous snake after the [[King cobra|king cobra]], and mature specimens generally exceed 2 m (6 ft 7 in). Despite the name, it is not black. The name refers to the inside of its mouth, which it displays when threatened. Its venom is primarily neurotoxic and is frequently fatal unless antivenom is given. The snake attacks humans only when threatened or cornered, and it is rated least concern by the International Union for Conservation of Nature.

Clandestine market or series of transactions that has some aspect of illegality. Illegal transactions include the [[Illegal drug trade|illegal drug trade]], [[Prostitution|prostitution]] where prohibited, illegal currency dealing and [[Human trafficking|human trafficking]]. Participants often conceal their activity from government authorities, and cash remains the preferred medium of exchange because it is harder to trace. Common motives include trading contraband, avoiding [[Tax|taxes]] or regulations, and evading price controls and rationing. The black market is distinct from the grey market, in which legal goods are distributed through unofficial channels. Black money, the proceeds of an illegal transaction on which taxes have not been paid, is often associated with money laundering. Because of its clandestine nature, the size of the underground economy cannot be determined. In the U.S., unreported income is estimated to be $2 trillion, resulting in a "tax gap" of $450–600 billion.

[[Spice|Spice]] made from the dried, cooked, unripe fruit of the flowering vine *Piper nigrum*. The vine is indigenous to the tropical evergreen forests of the Malabar Coast in southwestern [[India|India]], which was the ancient world's sole geographic source of the spice and became the center of early global trade. Black pepper is one of the most commonly traded spices in the world. Its pungency comes from the compound piperine, which differs from the [[Capsaicin|capsaicin]] of chili peppers. Black peppercorns are made by cooking the fruit briefly in hot water and then drying it, which darkens the skin into a thin, wrinkled layer. White pepper is made from the seed of the ripe fruit after the outer layer is removed. [[Vietnam|Vietnam]] is the leading producer, followed by [[Brazil|Brazil]] and [[Indonesia|Indonesia]], with annual world production estimated at approximately 500,000 metric tons as of 2023.

Type of tea that is more fully oxidized than oolong, yellow, white or [[Green tea|green tea]]. Black tea is made from the leaves of the shrub *Camellia sinensis* and is generally stronger in flavor than other teas. Unlike green tea, which usually loses its flavor within a year, black tea keeps its flavor for several years, so it became an article of trade; compressed bricks of black tea served as a form of de facto currency in [[Mongolia|Mongolia]], [[Tibet|Tibet]] and [[Siberia|Siberia]] well into the 19th century. Leaves are withered and then processed either by the orthodox method or by crush, tear, curl (CTC), and allowed to oxidize completely. The drink first originated in [[China|China]], where it is called *hong cha*, meaning red tea. Today black tea accounts for approximately 70% of total tea output as of 2024, with major producers including [[India|India]], [[Sri Lanka|Sri Lanka]], Kenya and [[Turkey|Turkey]].

English pirate who operated around the West Indies and the eastern coast of Britain's North American colonies. Also recorded as Edward Teach or Thatch, he is one of history's best-known pirates, though little is known of his early life. He sailed under Benjamin Hornigold before capturing a French slave ship, *La Concorde*, which he renamed *Queen Anne's Revenge* and armed with 40 guns, crewing it with over 300 men. His nickname came from his thick black beard, and he was reported to have tied lit fuses under his hat to frighten enemies. He blockaded the port of [[Charleston, South Carolina|Charles Town, South Carolina]] and ransomed its inhabitants. After accepting a royal pardon in North Carolina he soon returned to piracy, and he was killed by a force of sailors led by Lieutenant Robert Maynard at the battle of Ocracoke Inlet. He relied on his fearsome image rather than violence, and he became the inspiration for an archetypal pirate in fiction. The wreck of his flagship was discovered by divers in 1996 off North Carolina.

Edible fruit produced by many species of *Rubus* in the [[Rosaceae|rose family]]. The fruit is an aggregate of small drupelets, so botanically it is not a [[Berry (botany)|berry]]. Blackberry plants are perennial, bearing biennial canes: in the first year a new stem, the primocane, produces leaves but no flowers, and in the second year it becomes a floricane that flowers and fruits. Over 375 species are recognized, many of them closely related apomictic microspecies. Annual volumes of 20,000 pounds (9,100 kg) per acre (0.40 ha) are possible. The Himalayan or Armenian blackberry, *Rubus armeniacus*, is considered a noxious weed and [[Invasive species|invasive species]] in many regions of the [[Pacific Northwest|Pacific Northwest]] of Canada and the United States. Blackberry leaves feed certain caterpillars, and mammals disperse the seeds when they eat the fruit. Unlike a [[Raspberry|raspberry]], the torus stays with a blackberry when it is picked.

Medium-sized [[Antelope|antelope]] native to India and Nepal. It is the sole living member of the genus *Antilope*, described by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in 1758. It stands up to 74–84 cm (29–33 in) at the shoulder. Males have dark brown to black upper bodies and corkscrew horns 35–75 cm (14–30 in) long; females and juveniles are yellowish-fawn. Excessive hunting, [[Deforestation|deforestation]] and habitat destruction caused sharp declines in the 20th century, and small herds now largely survive in protected areas. Hunting is prohibited in India under the Wildlife Protection Act of 1972, and the species holds significance in [[Hinduism|Hinduism]].

Deciduous shrub in the family Grossulariaceae, grown for its edible berries. *Ribes nigrum* is native to temperate parts of central and northern Europe and northern Asia, where it prefers damp, fertile soil. It is winter hardy, but cold weather at flowering can reduce the crop, and [[Frost|frost]] below −1.9 °C (28.6 °F) can damage flowers. The raw fruit is particularly rich in [[Vitamin C|vitamin C]] and polyphenols. Blackcurrants are used in jams, preserves and syrups and are grown commercially for juice, and the fruit also flavors alcoholic beverages and dyes. Cultivation in Europe is thought to have started in the last decades of the 17th century. Plants are intolerant of [[Drought|drought]], and an established bush can produce about 4.5 kilograms (10 pounds) of fruit each year.

Casino banking card game, the most widely played such game in the world. It descends from a family of games known as twenty-one and uses decks of 52 cards. Players try to create totals higher than the dealer's without exceeding 21; number cards count at face value, face cards count as 10, and aces count as 1 or 11. A two-card total of 21 is called a 'blackjack' or 'natural.' The first written reference is in the work of [[Miguel de Cervantes|Miguel de Cervantes]], whose novella *Rinconete y Cortadillo* (written 1601–1602) describes card cheats playing the Spanish game veintiuno. Its immediate precursor was the English vingt-un, whose first rules appeared in Britain in 1800. The name 'blackjack' is linked to prospectors during the Klondike Gold Rush (1896–99), though French card historian Thierry Depaulis found no evidence for a bonus payout on an ace of spades and a black jack.

South Korean girl group formed by YG Entertainment, which debuted in August 2016. The four members are Jisoo, Jennie, Rosé and Lisa. Known for the 'girl crush' concept in [[K-pop|K-pop]], the group is regarded as a leading force of the Korean Wave. Its debut studio album, *The Album* (2020), was the first by a Korean girl group to sell one million copies, and *Born Pink* (2022) was the first to sell two million. Its Born Pink World Tour (2022–23) was the highest-grossing concert tour by a female group. Blackpink became the first Asian act to headline Coachella in 2023. With over 40 billion streams and 20 million records sold worldwide, it is one of the best-selling girl groups of all time.

Hollow muscular organ that stores urine from the [[Kidney|kidneys]] of [[Vertebrate|vertebrates]]. Urine enters the bladder through the ureters and exits through the [[Urethra|urethra]]. In humans the bladder sits on the pelvic floor and holds 300 to 500 ml (10 to 17 fl oz) before the urge to urinate occurs, though it can hold considerably more. Its detrusor muscle relaxes as the bladder fills and contracts during [[Urination|urination]]. Ridges of mucosal folds called rugae allow the bladder to expand, and flaps at the ureteric openings prevent urine from flowing back into the ureters. Storage and voiding are coordinated by nerves and centers in the [[Brainstem|brainstem]] and higher cortical areas. The Latin term for the organ is *vesica urinaria*.

1982 science fiction film directed by [[Ridley Scott|Ridley Scott]], adapted from [[Philip K. Dick|Philip K. Dick]]'s novel *Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?* [[Harrison Ford|Harrison Ford]] stars as a former police officer who hunts replicants, bioengineered humanoids. The film underperformed in theaters but became a cult classic and a foundational work of the [[Cyberpunk|cyberpunk]] genre. Seven versions exist, including *The Final Cut* (2007), the only version over which Scott retained artistic control. A sequel, *Blade Runner 2049*, was released in 2017.

French mathematician, physicist, inventor, philosopher and Catholic writer. Educated by his father, a tax collector, he wrote a treatise on conic sections at age 16 and corresponded with [[Pierre de Fermat|Pierre de Fermat]] on [[Probability theory|probability theory]]. In 1642 he began work on mechanical calculators, the Pascalines. He clarified the concepts of pressure and vacuum, and the [[Pascal (unit)|SI unit of pressure]] is named for him. Following Torricelli and [[Galileo Galilei|Galileo]], he rebutted the view that nature abhors a vacuum. He is credited with establishing the carrosses à cinq sols, the first modern public transport service. After a religious experience in late 1654 he wrote the *Lettres provinciales* and the *Pensées*, which contains [[Pascal's wager|Pascal's wager]], a probabilistic argument for believing in God.
